# Baruch Chapter 6 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
## [The Letter of Jeremiah]

**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Codex Vaticanus, Baruch 6 | **Source Image:** source-texts/greek-DC/BAR_006_page_001.jpg

---

**1** This is a copy of the letter that Jeremiah sent to the Judeans who were about to be marched off to Babylon as captives of the Babylonian king — carrying with it the message God had told him to give them.

**2** Because of the sins you have committed against God, you will be taken off to Babylon by Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon.

**3** Once you are there, you will stay for many years — a long time, as much as seven generations. After that, I will bring you out safely.

**4** Now, in Babylon, you will see gods made of silver and gold and wood, hoisted onto shoulders and paraded through the crowds, filling the nations with terror.

**5** Do not be like those foreigners. Do not let fear of their gods get its hooks into you

**6** when you see the throngs in front of and behind them, bowing down. Instead, say to yourself: You alone, O Lord, deserve to be worshipped.

**7** My angel is with you, and he is watching over your lives.

**8** Their tongues were shaped smooth by a craftsman, and they are plated with gold and silver — but they are fakes. They cannot speak a word.

**9** People bring them gold offerings as you would deck out a girl who loves jewelry —

**10** but the priests pocket the gold and the silver for themselves.

**11** They even hand some of it over to the prostitutes who work the temple roof, and they dress these wooden, gilded, and silvered idols in human clothing.

**12** But rust and moths do not respect purple robes — and these gods cannot protect themselves from either.

**13** Their faces have to be wiped, they are so thick with temple dust.

**14** One of them holds a scepter as if he were a judge over the country — but he cannot put to death anyone who wrongs him.

**15** He has a dagger in his right hand and an axe — but he is helpless against war and bandits.

**16** From all this it is plain: they are not gods. Do not fear them.

**17** A broken vessel is no use to anyone. In the same way these gods, once they are installed in their temples, can't even wipe the dust from their own eyes — the dust that the feet of visitors keep kicking up.

**18** A man condemned by the king has every gate locked against him. In the same way, the temple priests lock all the doors with bolts and bars — to keep robbers out, because the gods certainly can't stop them.

**19** They burn more lamps for these gods than they burn for themselves — but the gods can't see a single flame.

**20** They are like a wooden roof-beam. People say the life is eaten out of them. When the worms come up from the ground and gnaw at them and their clothing, they don't even notice.

**21** Their faces are blackened by the smoke that fills the temple.

**22** Bats, swallows, and birds roost on their heads and bodies. Cats too.

**23** So now you know: they are not gods. Do not fear them.

**24** All that gold they wear to look beautiful — unless someone polishes away the tarnish, it won't shine. And when they were being cast in the foundry, they felt nothing.

**25** They are sold for any price. There is no breath in them.

**26** They have no feet, so people carry them on their shoulders. And in being carried they display their own shame to everyone. Even those who serve them are humiliated.

**27** Set one down on the floor and it just stays there — it cannot get up. Tip it over and it cannot right itself. The offerings put before them are no different from offerings put before a corpse.

**28** What is sacrificed to them, the priests sell and pocket. Their wives take home some of the meat and salt it — but not a scrap goes to the poor or the helpless.

**29** Women who are menstruating and women in labor lay their hands on the sacrifices of these gods. Knowing all this — these are not gods. Do not fear them.

**30** What kind of gods need women for their priests? These wooden, silvered, and gilded things have women officiating at their shrines.

**31** Inside their temples the priests sit with their robes in tatters, heads and beards shaved, and nothing on their heads.

**32** They wail and shriek in front of their gods the way mourners wail at a funeral.

**33** The priests help themselves to the gods' garments and dress their own wives and children in them.

**34** Do good to one of these gods or harm it — it will not repay you either way. They cannot install a king or remove one.

**35** They cannot give you wealth or money. If you make a vow to them and break it, they will never call you to account.

**36** They cannot save anyone from death. They cannot rescue the weak from the powerful.

**37** They cannot give sight to a blind man. They cannot help someone in distress.

**38** They cannot show a widow any compassion. They cannot do a thing for an orphan.

**39** These wooden, gilded, and silvered idols are no different from the stones of a mountainside. Those who serve them will be put to shame.

**40** How, then, can anyone dare to call them gods?

**41** Even the Chaldeans show their contempt for them. When they see a mute person who can't speak, they bring him before Bel and ask Bel to give him speech — as if Bel had any understanding!

**42** But they can't see this themselves, so they don't walk away from the idols. They simply have no sense.

**43** There are women who sit along the roads wearing cords around their waists, burning bran as incense. When one of them is led off by a passing stranger and sleeps with him, she comes back and sneers at the woman next to her who hasn't yet been "honored" — whose cord hasn't been broken.

**44** Everything that goes on around these idols is a lie. How can anyone possibly call them gods?

**45** They were made by craftsmen and goldsmiths. The only thing they can be is whatever the craftsmen decided to make.

**46** And the craftsmen themselves don't live very long. So how could anything they make be a god?

**47** What they leave behind for future generations is nothing but falsehood and disgrace.

**48** When war or disaster strikes, the priests huddle together to figure out where to run and hide — taking the gods with them.

**49** How can anyone be in any doubt? These things cannot save themselves from war or disaster — they are not gods.

**50** They are made of wood, dressed in silver and gold. One day everyone will know it — every nation, every king will understand that they are not gods but man-made objects, with nothing of God in them.

**51** How can anyone not know they are not gods?

**52** They cannot set up a king over a country or send rain on the fields.

**53** They cannot settle a dispute. They cannot rescue someone who has been wronged. They have no power. They are like crows drifting between sky and ground.

**54** When fire breaks out in the temple of a wooden, gilded, and silvered idol, the priests run for their lives — but the idol gets burned along with the beams.

**55** And they cannot hold their own against a king or an army. How can anyone think they are gods?

**56** Wooden idols, silver-plated and gold-plated, cannot protect themselves from thieves and robbers.

**57** Anyone with more muscle than the idol can strip off its gold and silver and its fine clothing and walk away. The idol will not be able to do a thing.

**58** So — a king with actual courage is better than these gods. A kitchen pot that serves its owner's needs is better than these gods. A door that keeps the household safe is better than these gods. A wooden pillar in a palace is better than these gods.

**59** Sun and moon and stars are brilliant lights — and when they are sent on their errands, they go.

**60** Lightning blazes magnificently when it flashes; the wind sweeps across the whole earth.

**61** When God orders the clouds to move across the world, they obey.

**62** When fire is sent from heaven to burn down mountains and forests, it does what it is told. Not one of these idols can be compared to any of these things — not in how they look, not in what they can do.

**63** So neither think nor say that they are gods. They cannot judge cases. They cannot do good to human beings.

**64** Knowing that they are not gods: do not fear them.

**65** They cannot curse kings. They cannot bless them.

**66** They send no signs in the sky for the nations. They do not shine like the sun. They give no light like the moon.

**67** Wild animals are better off than these gods — at least animals can bolt to cover and look out for themselves.

**68** It is perfectly clear to us: they are not gods. Do not fear them.

**69** They are like a scarecrow in a cucumber field — protecting nothing. That is what these wooden, silvered, and gilded gods are like.

**70** Or like a white thornbush in a garden that every bird settles on. Or like a corpse thrown out in the dark.

**71** The purple and linen wrappings that rot on them will tell you plainly: they are not gods. In the end the idols themselves will rot, and they will be a disgrace throughout the land.

**72** Better, then, to be an honest person with no idols — for that person will never face this shame.

---
*PNEUMA notes: The Letter of Jeremiah is the funniest and most scathing piece of writing in the Deuterocanon. Its satirical strategy is relentless repetition — hammer after hammer, with the refrain ("they are not gods; do not fear them") landing every few paragraphs like a recurring punchline that also happens to be deadly serious. The rhythm has been preserved: the accumulating catalogue of indignities (rust, moths, birds, cats, temple prostitutes, stolen garments, useless scepters) builds to absurdity, then the refrain delivers the verdict. The final verse — "better to be an honest person with no idols" — drops the satirical register and speaks simply. The idol polemic has a long history (Jer 10, Isa 44, Ps 115) but Baruch 6 / Letter of Jeremiah takes it to its comic extreme.*
